q1263: God placed children together in families so they would learn, in a small and safe space, how to live with people who are different from them. The skills of sharing, negotiating, forgiving and making things right are learned at home before they are needed in marriage, church and work. That is part of His wise design. It also reflects His character. God loves each person fully and individually, without favourites, and He calls His family to unity, not uniformity. When parents give each child their own time and refuse to compare, children begin to feel secure enough to be generous. Over years, rivals can become friends, and many siblings become each other's closest companions through life.
q1264: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). Scripture treats sleep as a gift of trust. Proverbs 3:24 promises that when you lie down you will not be afraid, and your sleep shall be sweet. Psalm 121:3-4 says the One who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep, so a child can rest because God stays awake. Every evening Israel's priests spoke the blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 over the people. A short bedtime prayer and blessing carries this ancient pattern into your home. The Bible shows God as a watchful, near Father who makes it safe to close our eyes.
q1265: At bedtime the body needs to shift from alert to rest. Light, activity and excitement keep the brain alert, while darkness triggers the release of melatonin, a hormone that helps sleep begin. Screens give off bright light and stimulating content, and research suggests using them close to bed can delay sleep. Overtired children often seem wired because stress hormones rise to keep them going. Separation and lying alone with worries can also switch on the alarm system. A short routine that is the same every night tells the brain what comes next, which lowers stress. Talking about worries earlier, a comfort object and a promise to check back all signal safety. Over a week or two, predictable patterns help the body clock settle.
q1266: God built rhythm into creation, evening and morning, work and rest, and He built it into our bodies too. Children thrive on that rhythm because it lets them know the world is stable. Bedtime also teaches a deep spiritual lesson. Each night a child practises letting go of control, trusting that they will be watched over, and waking to new mercy. This is a little picture of how we all are meant to rest in God. A calm routine, a loving blessing and a parent who comes back when promised help children learn that being alone is not the same as being abandoned. In this way, God's design for sleep heals both body and heart.
q1267: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving" (1 Timothy 4:4). Scripture frames food as a gift to be received with gratitude, not a battle to be won. In Acts 2:46 the early believers ate together "with gladness and singleness of heart," and Ecclesiastes 9:7 invites us to eat our bread with joy. Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and He often revealed Himself at meals, breaking bread with friends and sinners. The table in the Bible is a place of welcome and peace. When parents remove pressure and focus on thankfulness and togetherness, they make meals a picture of God's generous provision.
q1268: Picky eating is very common between about two and six years old. Many researchers think a caution towards new foods once helped protect young children from eating something harmful. Children's taste buds are also more sensitive than adults', so bitter vegetables can taste stronger to them. Pressure, bribes and punishment raise stress, and stress tends to reduce appetite and increase resistance. When a child knows there is one safe food on the plate and they may decide how much to eat, the threat drops. Studies suggest it can take ten to fifteen relaxed exposures before a new food is accepted. Seeing parents enjoy varied foods, helping to cook and sitting at a calm table slowly teaches the brain that new tastes are safe.
q1269: God designed eating to be both nourishment and fellowship. He could have made us run on sunlight, but instead He gave us hunger, taste and the joy of sharing a meal. That design invites us to slow down, give thanks and enjoy one another. A child's cautious appetite is part of a protective design, and patience lets it open up in its own time. This reflects God's own patience with us. He keeps setting His good gifts before us without force, waiting for us to taste and see that He is good (Psalm 34:8). When the table is a place of peace, children learn to trust both their parents and their own bodies, which lays a healthy foundation for life.
q1270: "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time" (Ephesians 5:15-16). The Bible calls us to use our days with wisdom, and Psalm 90:12 asks God to teach us to number our days. Paul writes, "All things are lawful unto me, but I will not be brought under the power of any" (1 Corinthians 6:12). That is the heart of a healthy screen plan. Technology is not evil, but nothing should rule us except Christ. Philippians 4:8 directs our minds towards what is true, lovely and good. God guides His people with clear boundaries given in love, and He fills life with better things, not just prohibitions.
q1271: Many games, apps and videos are built to keep us engaged, using the brain's reward system. Each win, new level or notification can release dopamine, a chemical linked to wanting and motivation, so the brain keeps reaching for more. Children's self-control circuits are still developing, so stopping can feel like a real loss and lead to anger or tears. A five-minute warning and a timer give the brain time to prepare for a transition, and naming the feeling helps calm it. Keeping devices out of bedrooms protects sleep, which affects mood and learning. Research suggests that when real-life alternatives are appealing and parents model healthy use, children gradually find other sources of reward, and the battles usually ease over weeks.
q1272: God made us for real presence, faces, touch, creation, play and work with our hands. He designed the brain to find joy in these things, and that joy is meant to draw us towards Him and one another. Screens can offer good things, but they can also crowd out the slower rewards that build character and connection. Clear, kind limits are part of God's wisdom for our growth, just as the Sabbath protects us from endless work. When parents set a family plan together and follow it themselves, children learn that boundaries are not punishment but care. Over time they learn self-control, which Scripture calls a fruit of the Spirit, and they discover that life offline is rich.
q1273: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Colossians 3:23). Scripture gives work dignity and meaning, yet it also shows God helping people start what feels too big. Nehemiah rebuilt the wall section by section, each family doing the part near their own house. Proverbs 1:5 says a wise man will hear and increase learning, and Ecclesiastes 9:10 encourages us to do with our might whatever our hand finds to do. Philippians 4:13 reminds us that strength comes through Christ. God does not stand far off demanding results. He comes alongside, breaks the task into steps and strengthens us to keep going. Sitting beside your child reflects that patient help.
q1274: Homework refusal is often not laziness. The brain's ability to start a task, plan and focus, sometimes called executive function, is still developing in children and teens, and some children have learning difficulties or attention differences that make it harder. Fear of failure triggers the threat system, so the brain avoids the task to avoid the bad feeling. A snack and movement first restore energy and help the brain focus. Helping with the first question lowers the start-up barrier, and short chunks with breaks fit how attention naturally works. Praising effort, rather than intelligence, has been linked in studies with more persistence. Over weeks, a regular time and place builds a habit, so starting needs less willpower.
q1275: God designed people to grow through effort, practice and help from others. He could have given us knowledge instantly, but He chose to let us learn step by step, so that perseverance, humility and courage are formed along the way. Struggling with a hard task is part of how the brain grows and how character grows. The design also protects a child's worth. Grades are not identity. Each child is precious to God whether their marks are high or low, and parents reflect that when they keep their love separate from results. Working alongside a child and then stepping back mirrors how God helps us, giving enough support to begin, then trusting us to grow in strength.
q1276: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1). The Bible teaches that the way we speak shapes how others respond. "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6). James 1:19 asks us to be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, and Ephesians 6:4 warns parents not to provoke their children. Scripture also shows God allowing people to argue with Him. Abraham, Moses, Job and the psalmists all spoke honestly, and God listened, while still being God. He welcomes disagreement spoken in trust, and He corrects rebellion with patience. When parents answer rudeness calmly and set a clear boundary, they model the respect they hope to receive.
q1277: Rude words often come from a child who feels tired, embarrassed, powerless or unheard. In teens the brain is going through major changes, and the emotional areas can be very reactive while the brakes in the front of the brain are still developing. Children also copy the tone they hear. When a parent shouts back, both nervous systems move into fight mode and no one can listen. Staying calm and lowering your voice keeps your own thinking brain online and helps theirs settle. Taking a break, then returning to listen to the real issue, shows that disagreement is safe. With practice over weeks, children learn they can be heard without being disrespectful, and respectful disagreement becomes a habit.
q1278: God gave children a voice because He wants them to grow into people who can think, question and speak up for what is right. Back-talk is often a clumsy first attempt at that voice. The goal is not silence but respectful speech. This reflects God's character. He speaks to us with dignity, even when correcting us, and He invites our honest cries. When parents speak to children as they want to be spoken to, apologise when they are harsh, and give real choices, children learn that respect flows both ways. Over time the home becomes a place where disagreement does not destroy love. That prepares them for marriages, friendships and churches where truth is spoken in love.
q1279: "Be strong and of a good courage, be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Joshua 1:9). The Bible does not shame fear. It answers it with presence. "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" (Psalm 56:3) shows fear and trust side by side. Isaiah 41:10 promises God will strengthen and uphold us, and 2 Timothy 1:7 reminds us that God has given a spirit of power, love and a sound mind. Again and again God sent fearful people forward with Him, Moses, Gideon, Esther. He did not remove every hard thing first. He walked with them into it. That is the pattern for helping an anxious child take small brave steps.
q1280: Anxious children often have a sensitive alarm system. A part of the brain called the amygdala detects possible danger and signals the body to prepare, raising heart rate and breathing. Avoiding a feared thing brings quick relief, but research suggests avoidance teaches the brain that the thing really was dangerous, so the fear grows. Endless reassurance can have a similar effect. What helps is facing fears in small, manageable steps, often called a fear ladder, while a calm adult stays near. Slow breathing activates the body's calming system. Each brave step that goes well gives the brain new evidence of safety. Over weeks the alarm becomes less touchy, and children gain confidence that they can cope.
q1281: God designed the alarm system to protect us, and in a dangerous world it is a gift. In some children it is simply set very sensitive. God's way of healing fear is not to remove all challenge but to grow courage through His presence in the challenge. That is how He trained His people, and it is how He made the brain to learn. Courage is not the absence of fear but acting with fear while trusting someone stronger. When parents validate fear, show confidence and walk alongside, children learn this in their bodies. This design reflects God's patience. He does not rush us, and He celebrates small steps. Over time anxious children often grow into deeply compassionate and brave adults.
q1282: In the parable of the prodigal son, "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father did not pursue with lectures. He kept watching and was ready the moment his son turned towards home. God says through Isaiah, "Can a woman forget her sucking child? ... yet will I not forget thee" (Isaiah 49:15). Hosea 11:4 describes God drawing His people "with bands of love," and Psalm 139:7-10 says there is nowhere we can go where He is not with us. Scripture shows a God who gives space yet never withdraws love, always leaving a way back.
